KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Florida (CNN) -- So, what's harder, steering a space shuttle or out-machoing Tom Cruise on the set of "Top Gun"? Scott Altman is commander of the current space shuttle mission to upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope. Scott Altman laughs when he answers the question. "Flying a space shuttle is a little more challenging than what we did in the movie, although the flying was a lot of fun," said Altman, who knows more than a little about both. The retired Navy F-14 fighter pilot is the commander of the current space shuttle Atlantis mission to repair and upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope. He also doubled for the actors, including Cruise, during the Southern California shoot of the 1986 hit movie. Then a young pilot, Altman had just gotten back from a 7½-month tour onboard an aircraft carrier when he got the "Top Gun" call from his commanding officer. "The skipper of our squadron picked four guys he thought he could trust to have this kind of carte blanche to break the rules a little bit," Altman said. That included a scene in which a brazen Navy pilot buzzes the base's control tower. That would never happen in real life, Altman said. The movie features Cruise as a young naval aviator, Pete "Maverick" Mitchell, selected to attend fighter-pilot training school at the then-Miramar Naval Station north of San Diego. To prepare for the film, Cruise flew in the backseat of an F-14 several times, including once with Altman. "The actors were all pretty easy to get along with. Tom Cruise, for example, was very motivated," recalled Altman, who is making his fourth trip into space this week. "He enjoyed flying. He listened to what we told him and became a pilot himself after that." Altman is not one to brag about his flying in "Top Gun." The U.S. space agency, NASA, doesn't mention his film heroics, either. But Altman is in one of the movie's most memorable scenes. While flying upside down, inverted, Altman gives an obscene gesture to the pilot of an enemy plane. "They said go ahead and gesture at the other airplane," said Altman, 49, with a smile. "So when you're looking at the scene where he's communicating with the Russian, or the bad-guy pilots in the movie, that would be my finger." But the flying scenes with the actors didn't all work out as director Tony Scott had hoped. "The director had to pay $7,600 an hour to rent an airplane," Altman recalled. "But after a week of spending that much money on the airplanes, he decided he couldn't use the footage. The actors all looked a little green, he said." Altman and the other pilots earned $23 a day for their trouble. But his biggest disappointment was not getting to see the film as soon as it was released. He and the other pilots were invited to a preview screening, but a commanding officer would not let them go. And by the time the movie hit theaters, Altman was busy. He was overseas, on another seven-month tour of duty.

# From ‘Top Gun’ to Hubble: Scott Altman’s flight from Hollywood skies to space

**KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, Florida (CNN) —** Long before astronaut Scott Altman commanded a space shuttle on one of NASA’s most demanding missions, he was helping Hollywood create a different kind of high-flying spectacle.

As a young Navy fighter pilot, Altman flew F-14 Tomcats during production of the 1986 blockbuster “Top Gun,” performing aerial maneuvers that became part of the film’s signature flight sequences.

More than two decades later, Altman was back in the cockpit — this time at the controls of space shuttle Atlantis, leading seven astronauts on a mission to give the Hubble Space Telescope a new lease on life.

The two assignments shared some obvious ingredients: speed, precision and risk. But Altman said the realities behind the dramatic images depended on preparation and teamwork.

In May 2009, Altman commanded STS-125, the fifth and final shuttle mission devoted to servicing Hubble. Atlantis launched from Kennedy Space Center carrying replacement instruments, batteries, gyroscopes and other equipment for the orbiting observatory.

The mission was unusually complex. Unlike most later shuttle flights, Atlantis could not reach the International Space Station if its heat shield were damaged during launch. Hubble orbits on a different path, leaving the crew without the station as an emergency refuge. NASA placed another shuttle, Endeavour, on standby for a possible rescue.

Once Atlantis caught up with Hubble about 350 miles above Earth, the crew used the shuttle’s robotic arm to capture the school-bus-sized telescope and secure it in the payload bay.

Over five spacewalks, astronauts installed the Wide Field Camera 3 and the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph, replaced aging batteries and gyroscopes, and repaired two scientific instruments that had not been designed for servicing in orbit. The work required removing scores of tiny screws and handling delicate electronics while wearing bulky gloves.

Altman remained inside Atlantis, overseeing the choreography of the mission and maneuvering the shuttle as his crewmates worked outside.

The repairs transformed Hubble, restoring capabilities that allowed the telescope to peer deeper into the universe and study everything from distant galaxies to planets in the solar system.

It was a fitting assignment for a pilot whose career had repeatedly placed him at the intersection of advanced technology and human skill.

Altman graduated from the University of Illinois and entered the Navy, becoming an F-14 pilot and later a test pilot. During the filming of “Top Gun,” naval aviators performed the real flying while cameras captured the Tomcats in action. The actors may have supplied the dialogue and drama, but pilots such as Altman helped provide the film’s authenticity.

NASA selected him as an astronaut in 1995. He went on to fly four shuttle missions, first as a pilot and later as a commander. His spaceflight résumé included another Hubble servicing mission, STS-109 in 2002, giving him valuable experience before he took charge of Atlantis seven years later.

The final Hubble repair flight also carried an emotional weight. NASA’s shuttle program was nearing retirement, and no future crewed servicing mission to the telescope was planned. The astronauts knew that when they released Hubble back into orbit, they were likely saying goodbye on behalf of the entire shuttle program.

After the upgrades were completed, the crew used the robotic arm to lift Hubble from Atlantis and release it into space. The telescope drifted away, its new instruments ready to begin work.

Bad weather in Florida forced Atlantis to land at Edwards Air Force Base in California on May 24, 2009, ending a journey of nearly 13 days.

For Altman, the mission represented a career arc that would have seemed tailor-made for a movie script: from flying one of the Navy’s most recognizable fighters for Hollywood cameras to commanding a spacecraft sent to save one of humanity’s most important scientific instruments.

“Top Gun” made the F-14 a symbol of speed and swagger. Hubble demanded something quieter — patience, discipline and exacting coordination.

Altman had a hand in both.

counterfactuals.output:
Before Scott “Scooter” Altman became a four-time space-shuttle astronaut, he was a young Navy F-14 Tomcat pilot at NAS Miramar—the real “Fightertown USA”—when Paramount arrived to film *Top Gun*.

Altman was serving with Fighter Squadron 51, the “Screaming Eagles,” one of the squadrons that supplied airplanes, crews and pilots for the production. Because Tom Cruise, Val Kilmer and the other actors were not flying the Tomcats, Navy aviators performed the airborne maneuvers. Aircraft markings and editing then determined whether a particular Tomcat was supposed to be Maverick’s, Iceman’s or another character’s.

Altman later summarized his unusual acting career with variations of:

> “I was Maverick when he was flying.”

He also joked that he had doubled not only for Cruise but, depending on which aircraft the editors needed in a scene, for several of the other actors as well. He was not a conventional stunt double—his face did not replace theirs. He was the unseen pilot making their screen characters look like fighter aces.

### Flying for the cameras

Film flying was quite different from ordinary fleet training. Instead of simply winning a tactical engagement, Altman had to put the airplane where the camera aircraft could see it, hold precise relative positions and repeat maneuvers until the director had the desired shot. The pilots worked with camera-equipped aircraft and with the black-painted F-5s that portrayed the fictional Soviet “MiG-28.”

Altman flew a number of the movie’s most recognizable F-14 sequences, including high-speed passes, formation work, dogfighting and inverted flight. He has often been associated with the scene in which Maverick’s Tomcat rolls inverted above a “MiG” while Goose photographs the opposing pilot and the Americans engage in what Maverick calls:

> “Keeping up foreign relations.”

The famous gesture and the actors’ cockpit close-ups were filmed separately, but it took real Navy pilots—including Altman—to create the dangerous-looking, canopy-to-canopy encounter seen from outside.

Altman explained that movie work demanded an odd combination of precision and theatricality: maneuvers that felt dramatic to a pilot did not always look dramatic on film. The airplanes sometimes had to fly closer together, lower, or at a more camera-friendly angle than they normally would in a training exercise—always within whatever limits the Navy had approved.

### The tower flyby

One of Altman’s favorite stories concerned the high-speed, low-altitude pass that accompanies Maverick’s request for a tower flyby. The fictional controller refuses—“Negative, Ghost Rider, the pattern is full”—and Maverick goes anyway, sending an officer’s coffee flying.

Altman helped fly the real low passes used for such footage. His recollections emphasize that the production wanted the Tomcat as low and spectacular as possible, while Navy authorities imposed a minimum altitude. As he told the story, the first pass was not dramatic enough for the filmmakers, so subsequent passes became progressively more impressive. People near the runway quickly learned that an F-14 arriving at high speed and very low altitude was considerably more startling in person than on a movie screen.

The spilled coffee, of course, was Hollywood. The Tomcat thundering past was not.

### “Top Gun” and the astronaut interview

The film became part of Altman’s personal legend when he later applied to NASA. Astronaut-selection panels routinely pressed applicants to explain what distinguished them from the many other highly qualified military test pilots. Altman could point to combat-aircraft experience, test-pilot training and engineering credentials—but he also had an irresistible extra line on his résumé:

> “I was in *Top Gun*.”

He was fond of using that answer for comic effect, though his actual qualifications were formidable. NASA selected him in 1995. He went on to pilot shuttle missions STS-90 and STS-106 and to command STS-109, the fourth Hubble servicing mission, and STS-125, the fifth and final Hubble servicing mission.

Altman occasionally reflected on the contrast: in *Top Gun*, he flew an F-14 so movie stars could appear to be pilots; at NASA, he became publicly recognizable in his own right. Yet he remained amused that millions of people had watched his flying long before they knew his name. As he liked to put it, when viewers saw Maverick’s Tomcat maneuvering through the sky, at least some of the time:

> “That was me.”

# From ‘Top Gun’ to Hubble: Scott Altman’s two high-stakes cockpits

Before Scott “Scooter” Altman commanded a space shuttle on the final mission to repair the Hubble Space Telescope, he helped create a different kind of aviation spectacle: flying F-14 Tomcats for the 1986 movie “Top Gun.”

The two assignments placed Altman in some of the world’s most recognizable cockpits, but they demanded markedly different forms of precision. On the movie set, his flying had to be aggressive and visually dramatic while remaining safely within carefully planned limits. At NASA, every maneuver was governed by orbital mechanics, extensive checklists and the knowledge that there was little room for improvisation.

Altman, a U.S. Navy aviator and graduate of the Navy Fighter Weapons School popularly known as TOPGUN, was assigned to fly F-14s used in the film’s aerial sequences. Cameras recorded real fighters maneuvering over the Pacific, giving the movie an authenticity that helped turn it into a cultural phenomenon.

Although moviegoers saw Tom Cruise’s Pete “Maverick” Mitchell in the cockpit, experienced military pilots such as Altman performed much of the demanding flying captured for the screen. The work required pilots to put aircraft where cinematographers needed them, repeat maneuvers and account for camera planes, lighting and restricted filming windows.

That was a different challenge from combat training. A tactical maneuver is designed to defeat an opponent; a cinematic maneuver must also be visible and understandable to an audience. The pilot has to think not only about energy, altitude and spacing, but about how the aircraft will appear through a lens.

Altman later became a Navy test pilot, experience that more directly anticipated his NASA career. The agency selected him as an astronaut in 1994. He went on to fly four shuttle missions: as pilot of Columbia on STS-90 in 1998 and Atlantis on STS-106 in 2000, then as commander of Columbia on STS-109 in 2002 and Atlantis on STS-125 in 2009.

His shuttle assignments moved him from the fast, physically forceful world of naval aviation into the slower but more systemically complex environment of human spaceflight. An F-14 pilot could maneuver freely through three dimensions, often making rapid control inputs. The shuttle, by contrast, followed a tightly constrained path to orbit and returned as an unpowered glider.

Launch offered little resemblance to a movie dogfight. The shuttle’s computers controlled much of the ascent while the crew monitored systems and prepared to respond to failures. In orbit, success depended less on individual flying flair than on coordination among the astronauts, Mission Control and specialized teams on the ground.

The contrast became especially clear during Altman’s two Hubble servicing flights. STS-109 installed new equipment and replaced aging components on the observatory. Seven years later, Altman commanded STS-125, the fifth and final shuttle servicing mission to Hubble.

That 2009 flight was among NASA’s most demanding shuttle missions. Because Hubble’s orbit could not provide access to the International Space Station as an emergency refuge, another shuttle was prepared for a possible rescue. Altman’s crew captured the telescope with the robotic arm while spacewalkers repaired and upgraded instruments in a series of intricate excursions.

Yet the F-14 and shuttle chapters of Altman’s career shared a central requirement: disciplined teamwork. Neither “Top Gun’s” aerial footage nor a Hubble servicing mission could be accomplished by a lone pilot. Both relied on planners, engineers, maintainers, controllers and crews rehearsing complex operations before committing expensive machinery—and human lives.

Altman accumulated more than 51 days in space, but his brief connection to Hollywood remains an unusually visible footnote. Millions saw the results of his F-14 flying without knowing his name. Years later, millions more saw images from Hubble made possible in part by missions he commanded.

In one cockpit, Altman helped Hollywood portray the mythology of the fighter pilot. In the other, he carried out the less theatrical reality of spaceflight: methodical preparation, shared responsibility and exact execution under unforgiving conditions.

# From “Top Gun” to Hubble: The Astronaut Behind an Upside-Down F-14

Long before Scott “Scooter” Altman commanded a space shuttle, he helped create one of the most audacious images in 1980s cinema: an F-14 Tomcat flying upside down, canopy to canopy with an enemy fighter, while its crew snapped a photograph and offered a one-finger salute.

The scene in 1986’s *Top Gun* lasts only moments. Maverick and Goose roll their Tomcat inverted above a fictional MiG, close enough—at least according to Goose—to be “keeping up foreign relations.” Goose raises his middle finger, the camera clicks, and movie history is made.

Behind the aerial footage was Altman, then a young U.S. Navy fighter pilot and not yet an astronaut. He was among the naval aviators who flew F-14s for the production, and he has been widely credited with piloting the inverted Tomcat used in the famous sequence.

There is an important Hollywood distinction: Anthony Edwards, playing Goose, delivered the gesture seen in the close-up. Altman’s job was arguably harder. He had to put a large, expensive, supersonic fighter into the precise attitude filmmakers needed—while remaining safely within the limits set by the Navy and the realities of aerodynamics.

The result made recklessness look effortless.

That was the peculiar alchemy of *Top Gun*. Director Tony Scott’s film turned carefully planned military flying into a fantasy of instinct and rebellion. For the pilots involved, however, there was little room for improvisation. Camera angles could suggest two jets were nearly touching even when safety demanded far more separation. Every roll, pass and formation had to be coordinated by professionals who understood how quickly cinematic swagger could become catastrophe.

Altman was well suited to that world. Born in Lincoln, Illinois, in 1959, he studied aeronautical and astronautical engineering at the University of Illinois before entering the Navy. He became an F-14 pilot, graduated from the U.S. Naval Test Pilot School and accumulated thousands of hours in the air.

The movie was a colorful footnote in a career built on discipline rather than celebrity. A decade after *Top Gun* reached theaters, NASA selected Altman for its astronaut corps.

His first trip to space came in 1998 as pilot of shuttle *Columbia* on STS-90, the Neurolab mission. He flew again in 2000 aboard *Atlantis* on a mission to the International Space Station. Then came the assignments that would define his NASA career: commanding two missions to the Hubble Space Telescope.

On STS-109 in 2002, Altman led a crew that upgraded and repaired the orbiting observatory. Seven years later, he commanded STS-125, Hubble’s final servicing mission. The 2009 flight was unusually demanding. Because Hubble orbits far from the International Space Station, the shuttle crew could not simply seek refuge there if the spacecraft were badly damaged. NASA prepared a second shuttle for a possible rescue.

Altman and his crew nevertheless carried out the work, extending Hubble’s life and helping preserve one of the most productive scientific instruments ever built. The telescope went on delivering extraordinary views of distant galaxies, stellar nurseries and the deep universe.

The contrast is irresistible: the pilot associated with a cheeky middle finger in *Top Gun* later commanded missions devoted to humanity’s clearest view of the cosmos.

Yet the two chapters of Altman’s life were not as different as they might seem. Both depended on composure, technical mastery and trust. Flying inverted for a movie camera required far more than nerve. Commanding a shuttle demanded more than intelligence. In each case, success came from preparation so thorough that an extraordinary maneuver could appear almost casual.

Altman retired from NASA after four spaceflights and more than 50 days in orbit. By then, the young Navy pilot who had helped make Maverick look fearless had become an accomplished commander in his own right.

Millions remember the *Top Gun* scene for its irreverence: the inverted jet, the instant photograph, Goose’s grin and the obscene salute. Altman’s part is less visible. He was the steady hand behind the spectacle—the aviator who helped turn a carefully controlled maneuver into a symbol of cinematic bravado, then carried that same precision far beyond the atmosphere.

**Atlantis commander has a “Top Gun” Hollywood connection**

**CAPE CANAVERAL, Florida (CNN)** — Long before commanding the space shuttle *Atlantis*, astronaut Scott “Scooter” Altman helped create some of Hollywood’s best-known aerial scenes.

As a Navy F-14 Tomcat pilot, Altman participated in the filming of the 1986 movie *Top Gun*. He flew actor Tom Cruise several times during production and piloted aircraft used in the movie’s high-speed dogfighting sequences, including the famous inverted pass over an enemy fighter.

Paramount Pictures reimbursed the Navy about **$7,600 for each hour an F-14 was used**. The military pilots, however, received **no Hollywood bonus**; they continued to earn their normal Navy pay.

Altman and the other aviators were invited to a special preview of the film, but he never saw it. By the time it was screened, Altman was **away on an aircraft-carrier deployment**.

More than two decades later, the former “Top Gun” pilot traded his Tomcat for a spacecraft, commanding *Atlantis* on NASA’s final servicing mission to the Hubble Space Telescope.
